newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Hijack suspect alleges "repression" in Taiwan.
newsitem.headline: Hijack suspect alleges "repression" in Taiwan.

text.p: An unemployed journalist suspected of hijacking a Taiwan passenger plane to communist China on Monday alleged that he had faced political repression in Taiwan, airline executives said.
"The hijacker told the captain, 'I am a victim of political repression'," Lee Yun-ning, general manager of Far East Air Transport, whose aircraft was hijacked, told reporters in Taipei.

Lee said he had no further details of the complaint made by the suspect, identified by Taiwan authorities as 45-year-old jobless newsman Liu Shan-chung, described by former colleagues as an unreliable social misfit.

Far East Air Transport flight 128, a Boeing 757, had just taken off from southern Kaohsiung with 150 passengers and six crew at 0603 GMT when Liu doused himself with gasoline and ordered the captain to fly to Xiamen in southeast China, officials said.
The flight to the communist Chinese mainland touched off brief but intense military tensions.
Taiwan Defence Minister Chiang Chung-ling said four Taiwan fighters had scrambled into formation and tailed the plane part way across the Taiwan Strait.
Commanders decided not to intercept the flight so as not to incite a military "misunderstanding" with China's People's Liberation Army, a defence official told Reuters by telephone.

China has viewed Nationalist-ruled Taiwan as a rebel-held province since a civil war split them in 1949. China reserves a right to retake Taiwan by force and both sides have long kept their armed forces on high alert.
Liu was detained moments after the plane touched down.
Air piracy is a capital offence in China where he would be expected to be tried in the absence of clear agreements between Taiwan and China. The two have had no official contact since the civil war.
Taiwan media said Liu had served several years ago in Taiwan's army as a counter-intelligence officer and was a lieutenant colonel when he left the service in 1985.
Former colleagues and employers at three newspapers said Liu had been fired at least once and was known for problem drinking in the newsroom and emotionally volatile, anti-social behaviour.
"He was fired last summer after his alcoholism caused erratic behaviour," editor Yao Chih-hai of Kaohsiung's Commons Daily told Reuters by telephone from its head office.
Reporters at the east Taiwan newspaper Lientung Daily said Liu had worked there for just two months before leaving under a disciplinary cloud.
"He looked at first glance like an optimistic person, but we heard that his temper was pretty bad at times," one former co-worker said.
Former colleagues at the last newspaper where he worked, Modern Times, described him as a social misfit.
"He disliked everything he saw in society and often complained about many things," one Modern Times reporter said.
